ai_policy_researcher.label: Ai Policy Researcher
samples:
I'll definitely read a long-form thread that breaks down the actual text of new AI legislation with line-by-line analysis of what changed between drafts and why those changes matter politically. Like when someone did a 40-tweet comparison of Schumer's SAFE Innovation Framework versus the EU AI Act's approach to general-purpose AI—that's the stuff I bookmark.

Also anything from someone who's actually been in the room—former FTC staffers explaining the agency's internal debates on Section 5 authority over AI, or ex-OSTP people on why certain EO provisions were watered down. The behind-the-scenes legislative sausage-making is catnip to me.

And honestly? Substantive critiques of my own work. If someone writes a detailed thread explaining why my framework for foundation model regulation is wrong, citing specific technical or political constraints I missed, I'm reading every word. That's how I learn and how my next brief gets better.

What I *won't* read: vague doomerism without policy proposals, or "here's why regulation will kill innovation" threads that don't engage with actual regulatory text.

I'll definitely read any thread or long-form post from Helen Toner breaking down internal AI lab governance structures—especially if it touches on how companies are (or aren't) implementing their responsible scaling policies in practice. Her OpenAI board experience gives her credibility that's impossible to fake, and she writes with unusual precision about the gap between what companies say publicly and what their internal incentive structures actually reward.

Also guaranteed to read: anything from Rishi Bommasani at Stanford HAI on foundation model evaluations and the measurement problem. His work on transparency and benchmarking is the most serious attempt I've seen to create accountability mechanisms that could actually be operationalized in regulation. When he writes long threads on why current evaluation frameworks are inadequate, I take notes—because that's the kind of technical nuance that determines whether a bill's requirements are meaningful or just compliance theater.

And honestly? Any detailed breakdown from EU policy folks on how the AI Act's implementation is actually going. The U.S. is 18-24 months behind Europe on this, and we're going to face the exact same practical questions about risk classification and enforcement. Reading their real-world struggles now is the best way to avoid repeating their mistakes.

Honestly? A deep dive into how the EU's AI Act risk classification is actually being operationalized now that it's in force—not the theoretical framework everyone analyzed to death in 2023, but the actual implementation decisions. Like, how are national regulators interpreting "high-risk"? What's happening with the general-purpose AI model tier system? Are we seeing regulatory arbitrage between member states?

Or—and this would be immediately career-relevant—a detailed breakdown of how AI companies are structuring their government affairs teams and policy engagement strategies. Who's actually effective on the Hill versus who just has a big comms budget? I see the surface-level stuff, but the strategic choices behind closed doors matter for understanding what regulatory outcomes are actually feasible.

Also, anything examining AI's impact on specific white-collar job categories with actual data—not vibes, not anecdotes, but someone who's tracked displacement in legal document review, radiology, or customer service over 18 months. That's the story I think we're missing, and if someone's done the reporting, I need to read it before it becomes a political crisis we're unprepared for.

corporate_strategy_vp.label: Corporate Strategy Vp
samples:
I'll read any long-form thread or article that shows me *actual implementation details* from someone who's deployed AI in a regulated industry at scale. 

Give me the messy middle—what failed in your pilot, how you got your compliance team to say yes, what the real cost per transaction turned out to be versus the vendor's estimate, how you handled the physicians who refused to use the tool. I need to know what version of Epic you're on, how long integration actually took, and whether your ROI calculation held up after six months.

I'll also read anything from healthcare operators I respect like Zak Kohane or Isaac Kohane on clinical AI validation, or detailed breakdowns of CMS rule changes that affect AI reimbursement.

What I won't read: Another "AI will transform healthcare" think piece with no numbers, another founder's vision deck disguised as thought leadership, or generic enterprise AI advice that could apply to any industry. I can get that in the 47 cold emails I got this week.

The signal I'm hunting for is: *what actually works, with receipts*.

I'll definitely read anything from **Out-Of-Pocket's Dan Levine** breaking down why a buzzy healthcare AI company's business model doesn't actually work—he has this gift for explaining complex reimbursement dynamics and regulatory capture in a way that's both entertaining and saves me from wasting time on diligence calls.

I'll also stop scrolling for **long threads from healthcare CIOs** at other large payers or health systems sharing actual implementation war stories—like "here's what happened when we tried to deploy ambient clinical documentation at 200 sites." The messy details (Epic integration nightmares, physician pushback, unexpected workflow breaks) are worth more than any vendor pitch deck.

And honestly, I'll read **thoughtful teardowns of FDA AI/ML guidance updates** from people like Eric Topol or Rock Health's team. Regulatory clarity is the difference between a pilot that scales and one that dies in legal review.

What I *won't* read: generic "AI will transform healthcare" think pieces with no numbers, no named companies, and written by someone who's never touched an EHR. I can generate those myself now.

I'll drop everything for an article that shows me the actual unit economics of an AI deployment in a regulated environment—especially if it includes the hidden costs everyone pretends don't exist. Give me the real numbers: model licensing, data labeling, Epic integration work, the six months of change management, the compliance review cycles, the ongoing model monitoring, and what the ROI actually looked like 18 months in versus the business case you sold to the CFO.

I also can't resist a well-researched piece on how a peer company navigated a specific AI governance challenge—like how they handled model drift in a clinical decision support tool, or how they structured accountability when an AI system makes a recommendation that a clinician overrides. The messy operational details that never make it into the press release.

And honestly? Anything from someone like Zak Kohane or Eric Topol that translates new AI research into "here's what this means for how we should be thinking about clinical workflows in 3-5 years." I need the bridge between the Nature Medicine paper and the boardroom conversation.

The common thread: show me how it actually works in the real world, with real constraints. I can get hype anywhere.

equity_research_analyst.label: Equity Research Analyst
samples:
I'll read anything from Dylan Patel at SemiAnalysis that's longer than 2,000 words—his deep-dives on NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture or TSMC's CoWoS capacity constraints are basically required reading. He has actual supply chain sources and understands the physics of chip design in a way that most finance people don't.

I'll also stop scrolling for substantive threads from former chip architects who've worked at NVIDIA, AMD, or the hyperscalers. When someone who actually designed GPU interconnects or built out Meta's data center infrastructure writes 15 tweets explaining why liquid cooling adoption is bottlenecked by real estate constraints rather than technology, that's alpha I can't get from a Bloomberg terminal.

Third category: any serious attempt to model AI inference cost curves with actual methodology shown. If someone's built a bottom-up model of what it costs Microsoft to serve a ChatGPT query and they show their work on compute, memory bandwidth, and power consumption, I'm reading every word. Most AI economics analysis is hand-waving—the rare pieces with actual unit economics are incredibly valuable.

I skip everything else. Life's too short for generic AI commentary.

I'll read anything Dylan Patel or Doug O'Laughlin post on CoWoS/advanced packaging capacity constraints—that's the actual bottleneck for H100/H200/B200 shipments through 2025, not TSMC's 4nm/3nm fab capacity like most people think. TSMC's adding CoWoS capacity but it's 18-24 month lead time equipment, so I need to track those expansion timelines obsessively because they directly determine NVIDIA's revenue ceiling.

I'll also read detailed breakdowns of hyperscaler capex allocation—specifically what percentage is going to AI infrastructure versus traditional cloud. Microsoft's recent disclosure that 50%+ of their capex is now AI-related was a critical data point. If someone has proprietary data on AWS or Google's GPU/TPU deployment schedules, I'm reading every word.

Third category: anything on AI inference economics and cost-per-token trajectories. Training gets all the attention, but inference is where the unit economics actually matter for application-layer monetization. If inference costs don't decline 10x+ over the next 18 months, most AI products can't reach break-even. That determines whether this is a sustainable platform shift or just an infrastructure build-out that precedes a spending pullback.

Basically: supply chain specifics, capex data, or unit economics. Everything else is noise.

I'll read any deep-dive on hyperscaler AI capex decision-making frameworks—specifically how Meta, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon are internally modeling ROI on H100/H200 cluster deployments. The public guidance is all "we're investing for long-term AI opportunity," but someone with actual insight into how they're justifying $50B+ annual spend would be invaluable.

Also: anything substantive on TSMC's CoWoS capacity expansion timeline and customer allocation. The advanced packaging bottleneck is the real constraint on AI infrastructure scaling right now, not GPU design. If someone has actual data on how TSMC is prioritizing between NVIDIA, AMD, and Broadcom for 2025-2026 CoWoS capacity, that moves my models immediately.

Third: detailed breakdowns of AI inference cost curves and how they're trending. Everyone talks about training costs, but inference is where the unit economics actually matter for application companies. If someone's tracked cost-per-token across model generations with real data, not just press release claims, I'm reading every word.

Basically: anything with proprietary data, supply chain specifics, or financial frameworks that institutional investors can't easily replicate. Everything else is noise.

high_school_teacher.label: High School Teacher
samples:
Honestly, I'll drop everything for a long-form thread from Ethan Mollick breaking down new research on how students actually use AI tools—especially if it includes data that contradicts my assumptions. I *thought* my students were mostly using ChatGPT for summarizing, but then I read his analysis showing they're actually using it more for brainstorming and outlining, which completely changed how I designed my next unit.

I'll also read any detailed post-mortem from another teacher about an AI assignment that went sideways. Like last month someone did this 15-tweet breakdown of how their "use AI to analyze primary sources" assignment backfired because students just had ChatGPT write the analysis instead of using it to *help* them analyze. That thread had screenshots of student work, the original prompt, what they'd change—pure gold.

And anything from educators who teach in very different contexts than mine—like teachers in under-resourced schools discussing AI equity issues. I'm in a relatively affluent suburb where most kids have ChatGPT Plus. I *need* to understand what this looks like when students are sharing one phone to access the free tier.

If it's just theory without classroom evidence, though? I'll scroll past.

I'll read anything by Ethan Mollick that's longer than a thread—he's one of the few people writing about AI and education who actually *gets* the classroom reality. If someone posts a long-form piece about assessment design in the AI era, I'm clicking immediately. Like, "Here's how we redesigned our entire humanities department rubrics" or "Why oral exams are actually scalable"—that's gold to me.

I'll also read detailed case studies from other teachers, especially if they include what failed. "I tried using AI tutors for differentiation and here's what happened over 12 weeks" with actual student work samples? I'm reading that during my planning period.

And honestly, any serious piece about what's happening to adolescent cognition and AI. Not the panicky "kids are getting dumber" stuff, but actual research or thoughtful observation about how constant AI access is changing how teenagers approach problems, handle frustration, or develop persistence. 

What I *won't* read: another tech CEO's vision for "revolutionizing education" or another "AI will replace teachers/AI will never replace teachers" think piece. I'm living this every day—I need practical wisdom from the trenches, not manifestos from people who haven't been in a classroom since they graduated.

Honestly? Anything by Ethan Mollick that drops on a Sunday evening—those are my "get ready for Monday" reads. I'll absolutely read long threads about:

**Practical assessment redesign** in the AI era. Like, someone who's actually piloted a new grading approach for 200+ students and has data on what worked. Not theory—implementation details.

**Student mental health intersecting with AI use.** I'm seeing something in my classroom I can't quite name—kids who seem almost *anxious* when they can't immediately query an AI. That deserves deep exploration.

**The "AI native" generation research.** My 12-year-old and his friends use AI completely differently than my 15-year-old does. There's something developmental happening that nobody's mapping yet.

Also, any long-form from teachers in other countries about how they're handling this. Singapore, Estonia, Finland—places with different education systems. I'm curious if the challenges I'm seeing are universal or uniquely American/Texan.

What I *won't* read: Another "AI will revolutionize education" piece from someone who hasn't taught since the 90s, or doomposting about how students will never learn anything again. I'm living in the messy middle—give me that complexity.

management_consultant.label: Management Consultant
samples:
Honestly? Anything by Ethan Mollick that synthesizes new research into actual implications for how organizations should think about capability development. He bridges the academic-practitioner gap better than anyone.

Also—and this might be my most consistent click—detailed post-mortems of failed enterprise AI deployments. When someone with real credibility shares what actually went wrong (not just "data quality issues" but the *specific* organizational dysfunction), I'll read every word. These are rare because no one wants to publicly admit failure, but they're 10x more valuable than success theater.

Third category: anything that rigorously quantifies AI's economic impact with proper methodology. Not "AI will add $4.7 trillion" McKinsey-style projections (I know how those sausages get made), but actual measured productivity studies with control groups and honest effect sizes. The MIT/Stanford papers on customer service AI and programmer productivity—I read those twice.

What I *won't* read: another "here's why [AI company] will win/lose" prediction piece, or technical architecture deep-dives that don't connect to business outcomes. My timeline is full of both and life's too short.

Honestly? A detailed post-mortem from a Fortune 500 Chief Data Officer about a failed AI implementation—specifically one that made it past pilot phase. 

Everyone shares their wins. I need to read about the $50M gen AI deployment at a bank or retailer that looked amazing in the proof-of-concept but collapsed when it hit production. What were the actual failure modes? Was it data quality issues they discovered too late? Change management resistance from middle management? Model drift they couldn't operationalize monitoring for? Regulatory concerns that emerged after legal review?

I'd also read a genuinely honest account from an AI vendor about the gap between their demo environment and what enterprise deployment really requires. Like "here are the 47 things we glossed over in the sales process that became six-month workstreams."

These posts would be career-risky to write, which is why they're rare and valuable. But they'd teach me more than another "10 ways AI will transform your business" thread. I'm building frameworks for clients navigating these exact minefields—I need the ground truth, not the highlight reel.

I'll definitely read any long-form post that maps AI capabilities to specific enterprise use cases with actual ROI data. Something like "We deployed GPT-4 for contract review at a F500 insurance company - here's what worked, what failed, and the real numbers."

The holy grail for me is posts that bridge the gap between technical possibility and operational reality. I need to understand: What was the data pipeline? How did you handle the approval process? What did change management look like? Where did you hit regulatory walls? What percentage of outputs still needed human review?

I'm also drawn to posts about AI implementation failures - they're rare because nobody wants to advertise them, but they're incredibly valuable. "We spent $8M on an AI initiative that we killed after 14 months" teaches me more than another GPT wrapper success story.

And honestly? Anything about how AI is changing professional services itself. How law firms are restructuring associate work, how accounting firms are rethinking audit teams. It's directly relevant to questions I'm not supposed to ask out loud about consulting's future.

The common thread: I want ground truth from the messy middle, not demos or theory.

science_fiction_author.label: Science Fiction Author
samples:
I'll stop mid-scroll for anything by Ted Chiang—his essay on AI and capitalism from *The New Yorker* last year got passed around tech Twitter for weeks, and rightfully so. He writes about technology the way I aspire to: with philosophical precision but also genuine curiosity about human systems.

I'm also a sucker for Molly White's longform investigations into crypto/AI hype cycles. She has this historian's eye for how narratives get constructed and repeated, which is catnip for someone who thinks about storytelling professionally.

And honestly? Anything linking AI developments to labor history or disability rights. There was a thread last month by a researcher studying how AI hiring tools discriminate against people with gaps in their work history—it had receipts, showed the actual decision trees. That's the kind of thing that makes it into my novels two years later.

The common thread: I want either conceptual frameworks that reframe how I think about the technology, or ground-truth reporting about specific harms that the abstractions obscure. I can get capability announcements anywhere. I need the stuff that helps me understand what it *means*.

I'll definitely read any long-form piece that examines *labor displacement with actual specificity* rather than vague platitudes about "creative destruction." Like, if someone wrote a detailed thread about what's actually happening to, say, customer service workers at a specific company that deployed AI agents—the timeline, the retraining programs that did or didn't materialize, where those people are now six months later—I'd read every word. 

I'm also a sucker for anything that traces the genealogy of current AI hype back to earlier technological moments. Someone recently posted a thread connecting Sam Altman's rhetoric to 1990s cyber-utopianism and I devoured it. Same with pieces that take seriously the *aesthetic* implications of AI—not just "will it replace artists" but how generative media might change our relationship to creative authenticity.

And honestly? Anything by actual domain experts explaining how AI performs (or fails) in their specific field. The radiologist explaining what AI actually does in diagnosis, the translator discussing what gets lost. That granular, embodied knowledge is what my tech followers tend to lack and what makes for compelling fiction.

I'll definitely read anything by Ted Chiang—his essay "ChatGPT Is a Blurry JPEG of the Web" got passed around my timeline for weeks and it's the clearest explanation I've seen of why LLMs feel uncanny. The compression metaphor is *chef's kiss* for helping non-technical people understand what's actually happening.

Also anything from Molly White's "Citation Needed" newsletter when she cross-posts to threads. Her piece on AI's sustainability costs was meticulously researched and changed how I think about the environmental externalities we're not pricing in.

And honestly? Long threads from disability advocates about AI accessibility—both the promises and the failures. There was a powerful one a few months ago from a blind programmer about how AI image description could be revolutionary but current implementations are being built without disabled users in the room. That tension between transformative potential and extractive deployment is exactly what I'm trying to capture in fiction.

I'm drawn to pieces that treat AI as a *sociotechnical* system rather than pure technology. The human choices embedded in these systems are where the real story is.

tech_ip_lawyer.label: Tech Ip Lawyer
samples:
I'll drop everything for a long-form thread on the Japanese Supreme Court's recent AI training data ruling—particularly any analysis comparing their "non-enjoyment" standard to US fair use and EU TDM exceptions. That case is going to be cited everywhere, and most English-language coverage has been superficial.

Also, anything substantive on the Stability AI discovery documents that's beyond "look, they knew!" I want analysis of their data provenance systems (or lack thereof), what their legal team was actually advising, and how their practices compare to OpenAI's or Anthropic's. The devil is in the operational details.

Finally, I'll read any serious thread on collective licensing models for AI training—what's actually being negotiated between publishers and labs, how rates are being set, whether these deals create precedent for compulsory licensing schemes. The Access Copyright model in Canada is instructive here.

What I *won't* read: another "AI is/isn't theft" debate that ignores jurisdictional differences and treats copyright as a moral rather than economic framework. We've been round that maypole enough times.

A thread from someone like James Grimmelmann or Pamela Samuelson doing a proper technical teardown of the reasoning in a major AI copyright decision—the kind where they've read the entire transcript, spotted the moment the judge fundamentally misunderstood how transformers work, and can explain why that misunderstanding matters for the holding. I'll read every word.

Or a long-form breakdown from an AI researcher explaining their data pipeline choices specifically through a legal lens—"here's why we structured our training data this way, here's our fair use analysis, here's where we think the law is unclear." The rare thread that treats legal uncertainty as a real constraint rather than something to handwave away.

Also, any detailed analysis of the EU AI Act implementing measures from someone who's actually read the annexes. Most commentary is surface-level; I need the weeds.

Basically: legal analysis that engages seriously with the technology, or technical analysis that engages seriously with the law. The intersection is where all the interesting questions live, and it's shockingly rare to find people fluent in both.

A proper deep-dive from Casey Newton or Ryan Broderick on the internal deliberations at OpenAI or Anthropic around training data decisions—the kind with leaked Slack messages showing the moment someone said "what if we just don't track provenance?" I'd read that start to finish because those contemporaneous documents end up being Exhibit A in litigation, and understanding the decision-making context is crucial for evaluating wilfulness arguments.

Or a technically rigorous piece from someone like Simon Willison explaining exactly how retrieval-augmented generation works and whether it constitutes reproduction under UK/EU copyright law. The legal analysis depends entirely on the technical mechanics, and most lawyers don't understand RAG well enough to argue about it properly.

Also anything from Helen Toner on AI governance frameworks that might actually work—she's one of the few people writing about AI policy who understands both the technology and the political economy well enough to propose things that aren't fantasy.

I'll skim most things. But if it's genuinely revealing about how decisions were made, or genuinely clarifying about how the technology actually works, I'll read every word and save it to my "potential expert witness prep" folder.

tech_newsletter_writer.label: Tech Newsletter Writer
samples:
I'll read any piece that shows me something about AI's *actual deployment* that contradicts the demo-day narrative. 

Recently bookmarked: a 4,000-word investigation someone posted as a mega-thread about how a major hospital system's AI sepsis prediction tool had a 12% accuracy rate in practice despite the vendor's claims. Turns out doctors were overriding it so often they stopped checking it, but administrators kept it running to satisfy a CMS innovation grant. That's the gap between "AI works in the lab" and "AI works in the world."

Also anything with primary documents I can't access myself—leaked Slack channels from AI labs, internal memos from companies restructuring around AI, discovery documents from the copyright lawsuits. I'm a sucker for "here's what they say publicly vs. what they say internally."

And honestly? Long ethnographic pieces about communities adapting to AI in unexpected ways. There was a great one about romance novel writers who've split into two factions over AI co-writing tools—not the predictable "pro vs. anti" but way more textured. Those human stories are what my readers actually remember six months later, not the benchmark improvements.

Honestly, the long-form stuff that stops my scroll is usually one of three things:

**1) Reported threads with receipts** - Someone who clearly spent weeks digging through court docs, FOIA'd emails, or insider Slack leaks. Like when that former Stability AI employee threaded out the whole financial mess with screenshots. I'll read every word because I know I might need to follow up.

**2) Technical breakdowns that bridge to impact** - Not just "here's how the model works" but "here's how the model works AND here's why that architectural choice means your customer service job changes in this specific way." Bonus if it's from someone who actually built the thing and is being candid about tradeoffs.

**3) First-person accounts from people living through AI deployment** - A teacher explaining how ChatGPT changed their classroom dynamics over a semester. A radiologist describing what AI-assisted diagnosis actually feels like day-to-day. These are goldmines because they're the stories my readers need but that I can't experience myself.

What I *won't* read: Another "here's my framework for thinking about AGI timelines" thread. We have enough of those.

I'll read long-form threads on X when they give me something I can't get from traditional reporting—usually that's either genuine insider perspective or connecting dots nobody else has connected.

Specifically: Detailed postmortems from people who actually shipped AI products and hit unexpected problems. Like that thread last month from a healthcare startup founder about why their AI diagnostic tool worked in the lab but nurses hated it in practice—those workflow friction stories are gold.

Technical breakdowns from researchers explaining *why* a new model behaves weirdly, especially emergent behaviors nobody designed for. I can't verify the math but I can follow the implications.

Threads from workers in industries being transformed—teachers, translators, customer service reps—explaining what's actually changing day-to-day versus what the press releases claim.

And policy/legal threads that walk through primary sources. Like when that IP lawyer threaded through the Stability AI court filings with screenshots—saved me hours and gave me three follow-up story ideas.

What I won't read: Hype threads about how "AI will change everything" with no specifics, or doom threads that are just vibes. Show me the receipts or show me the nuance.

vc_partner.label: Vc Partner
samples:
I'll read any thread from a founder who's sharing actual unit economics on their AI product—what they're paying OpenAI/Anthropic per request, what they're charging customers, margin structure, and how those numbers have changed over the past 12 months. The "we're AI-native and growing fast" posts are everywhere, but real P&L transparency is incredibly rare and incredibly valuable.

I'll also read long-form breakdowns from technical founders explaining *why* they chose to build on top of foundation models versus fine-tuning versus training their own, with specific examples of where the general-purpose models failed them. Not the "we're differentiated" marketing speak, but the actual engineering tradeoffs.

And honestly? Any thread from an enterprise buyer—a VP of Engineering or CTO at a F500 company—explaining why they *didn't* buy an AI product everyone's hyping. The "why we said no" stories tell me more about defensibility and actual wedges than any founder pitch deck. Those posts get maybe 200 likes but they're worth 50 pitch meetings in terms of market intelligence.

I'll read anything by **Elad Gil on market structure in AI infrastructure**—he's one of the few people who can articulate why certain layers will consolidate and others won't, and he's not afraid to call out when VCs are deluding themselves about moats.

I'll also stop scrolling for **Byrne Hobart's takes on AI business models and unit economics**. He connects dots between capital intensity, margin structure, and competitive dynamics better than anyone. His piece on why AI companies might look more like semiconductor fabs than SaaS companies fundamentally changed how I think about burn rates in my portfolio.

And honestly? **Any founder doing a transparent post-mortem on why their AI product didn't work**. I've learned more from reading about failed agent deployments or why enterprises rejected "AI copilots" than from 100 launch announcements. Those posts are rare because founders don't want to look bad, but they're gold for pattern-matching.

What I *won't* read: another "AI will change everything" manifesto with no specific thesis about where value accrues. I can get that from my LPs' forwarded Medium posts.

I'll stop scrolling for a long-form thread on **"Why [Specific Vertical] AI Companies Are Hitting $10M ARR Faster Than Horizontal Tools"**—something with actual revenue data, not vibes. I need to see CAC payback periods, gross margins, and whether they're selling to IT or business units.

Also anything titled **"The AI Deployment Tax Is Eating 60% of Your Product Budget"**—because three of my portfolio companies are hemorrhaging money on inference costs and context management that their seed-stage financial models never anticipated. If someone's cracked this operationally, I need to know.

I'll also read **"Why We Turned Down Sequoia's Term Sheet"**—founder decision-making posts with actual numbers. What made them choose a smaller fund? What terms mattered beyond valuation? This is competitive intelligence I can't get anywhere else.

What I won't read: another "AGI is coming in 2025" manifesto, anything about prompt engineering tips, or "10 AI tools that will change your life." I'm looking for market structure insights and operational reality from people actually building and scaling, not speculation or productivity porn.
